utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, good morning, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. If I may introduce, please, Ms. Shokriya Majidi, who is originally from Afghanistan and has been working with my team for the last four months. She's a graduate of the University of The Hague. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's been some time since the last meeting of ours and my pleasure to see you in good health and spirit. I'm going mostly to address you neither in Serbian nor in Japanese but in English, which is a real winner of the 20th century wars. Nevertheless, we have to wait for the two translations in Serbian and in French. Excellency, may I ask you for the record to tell us -- to tell the Chamber in short your date and place of your birth, and full name, of course, and name of father.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Karadzic, for your kind greetings. I think we spent a very difficult time together in the former Yugoslavia. My name is Yasushi Akashi. My date of birth is 19th of January, 1931.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you be kind to shortly, which is not going to be easy, review your career and tell it for the record and for the sake of Chamber's knowledge.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: My career has been long, and I have to make a short capsule of it. I was brought up in Japan, was educated there, graduating from the University of Tokyo in 1954. I then went to the United States as a Fulbright Scholar and started at the University of Virginia and then at the Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy. I then joined the UN in February 1957, worked at the department of political and Security Council affairs. And from 1974 to 1979, I worked at the Japanese mission to the UN as a councillor, minister, and then as ambassador. I then rejoined the UN as Under-Secretary-General for public information, subsequently as Under-Secretary-General for disarmament affairs, and then I was appointed the Secretary-General's Special Representative for UN peacekeeping in Cambodia. That was 1992. I completed my assignment there in a year and a half. I went back to UN headquarters, then I was appointed SRSG [Realtime transcript read in error "SISG"] for the former Yugoslavia. In January 1994 and until end of October 1995, I was back at the UN headquarters then, and I was special advisor to the Secretary-General. Afterwards, I was made Under-Secretary-General for humanitarian affairs until I retired from the UN from -- at the end of 1997. I went back to my country, Japan, and have been engaged in quite a number of jobs, mostly in the non-governmental area, but I have a part-time responsibility with the government as the representative of the Japanese government on peace building in Sri Lanka, and I'm the head of the international house of Japan and some other non-governmental responsibilities dealing with international affairs and trying to promote peace and reconciliation between Japan and some of the neighbouring countries of Japan. That I think that more or less summarises.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. For transcript page -- Ambassador, if you could take a look at line 2 in the transcript. Should "SISG" not read "SRSG," Special Representative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency. It was not as easy to present this remarkable career. May I ask you, Excellency, taking into account that this mission in Yugoslavia was not the first such operation, were you -- were there any doubts of implementing the peacekeeping operation in Yugoslavia, and if on what basis, in the United Nations and among the big powers?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I myself divide the UN peacekeeping operations into several different categories. The -- our operation in Cambodia is what I call second-generation peacekeeping. The first generation started in 1949 in the Middle East with UN truce supervisional organisation which was deployed on the cease-fire lines or truce lines between Israel on the one hand and neighbouring Arab states on the other. That's the first-generation peacekeeping. UN role was limited to mostly strategic supervisory job of verifying cease-fire lines or truce lines or national borders, but with the Cambodian peacekeeping, the second-generation peacekeeping started in 1992. This generation is a multidimensional peacekeeping involving not just strategic advisory functions but more dynamic complex functions extending from military to political, economic, and reconstruction work. So Cambodia was a very complex, very large peacekeeping. It's a military component towards itself over 20.000 people. But the -- what I call the third-generation peacekeeping is the UN operation in Somalia which delved into the more forceful operation in accordance with Secretary-General Boutros-Ghali's doctrine enunciated in the agenda for peace, his own special report to the Security Council. And in the mid-1990s, UN was confronted with three very major, unprecedented challenges: In Somalia, in Rwanda, and in the former Yugoslavia. And in all cases, UN experienced very serious difficulties, and we wondered whether our traditional definition of our responsibility and tasks was sufficient or not, especially in the former Yugoslavia. UN Security Council issued more resolutions and precedential statements than in any other previous peacekeeping operations, but I don't think anybody should judge it's productivity by the number of resolutions or statements adopted. The basic trouble with UNPROFOR in the former Yugoslavia was lack of unity of opinions or viewpoints in the Security Council. In Cambodia, we were fortunate to have modest unity of outlook in the international community effected in Security Council, but in the former Yugoslavia at least three different viewpoints prevailed, even among the five permanent members of the Security Council. So our work was made very difficult, very controversial, and yet under the direction of the UN Secretary-General, I must say that all of us in UNPROFOR did our very best to fulfil our responsibilities to the UN to the best of our ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have in the e-court document 1D10513.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, did you give an interview in French parliament?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes. It was not a full chamber of the French parliament but one of its committees, I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we see page 5.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you, Dr. Karadzic, repeat the document's number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, this is a number in e-court but this is your interview in this committee of French parliament, and page in this document is 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps, Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Akashi could be advised that the translation of that document appears on the screen in front of him, and you could ask him if he's able to see it at the size it is and recognise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we show the witness the first page of this document first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you make the letters a bit larger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And then shall we move to the relevant page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, please. Page number 5.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Letters can be made larger? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, this is chapter number 2, nature of UN peacekeeping in former Yugoslavia. What you have been telling before we called this document, is it in this page concerning those doubts about implementing peacekeeping operation in Yugoslavia and about the premature or selective recognition? Could you tell us about this statement of yours on this subject.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes. In a sense, I think we can say that UN peacekeeping operation in the former Yugoslavia was imposed on the UN. The Secretary-General of the UN at that time was Mr. Perez de Cuellar and he felt serious doubts about the wisdom or even the possibility of UN carrying out responsibilities in the former Yugoslavia. His principal advisor on this question was Cyrus Vance, American Secretary -- former American Secretary of State, highly respected diplomat, and both of them felt that in the volatile conflict in the former Yugoslavia, UN peacekeeping operation is not suitable as a useful instrument for peace. UN peacekeeping, as the name suggests, is for the purpose of keeping peace, not to create peace. So -- but in the former Yugoslavia, actual fighting was ongoing, so there was no cease-fire agreement, no peace agreement either. So there was, in short, no [Realtime transcript read in error "in"] peace to keep. So UN Secretary-General and others in the UN had serious doubts about UN going into former Yugoslavia, but in a sense European countries exerted pressures on the UN to step in despite these lingering doubts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency. You underlined the lack of consensus between the three parties, warring parties, in Bosnia, but also you, in comparison to the Cambodia case, you underlined the lack of accord among the great powers concerning the war in former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could we see lower part of this page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And may ask you, Excellency, just to explain your view on those differences and how those differences affected ending of the war -- the course of the war and ending of the war.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Here we have to take into serious account the state of public opinion in the world as reflected by media's, mass media's, viewpoints. Much of mass media in the world were horrified by the tragedy of -- and the seriousness of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia, and they called for some action to bring about alleviation of this conflict, especially in the humanitarian area, to alleviate the suffering of the innocent people. And also for Europeans in particular, I think they were anxious to stem the tide of inflow of refugees, large number of refugees, from the former Yugoslavia. So the government were in many ways compelled to do something in order to respond to the voices of public opinion and many media's cries. So I think the -- because of the complexity of the conflict and existence of plurality of viewpoints, the Security Council puzzled over actions to take, and many of their actions by the nature of the Security Council were based on a compromise, and result of compromise was often times the -- the ambiguousness of the resolutions and the precedential statements adopted, and this made the actual task of implementing these decisions and the resolutions by the peacekeepers on the ground exceedingly difficult, and some generals in our peacekeeping said that they read resolutions and statements in -- from the Security Council many, many times and could not understand what they meant. And so they told me that they stopped reading those resolutions, which did not in their opinion make sense. So this was a perplexity in which many of my colleagues in New York as well as on the ground were faced with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I tender this document, this page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "This page" meaning page 5?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Cover page and front page and page 5 for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How about chapter 2 of this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Chapter 2 being how many pages, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Chapter 2 being pages 5 and 6 in part of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber has no difficulty with it. We'll admit the cover page and the chapter 2.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3488, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And just for the record, transcript page 7, line 8, should read "So there was, in short, no peace to keep," instead of "in peace." Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, did you see the reason or reasons why the peace was not achieved earlier or, rather, in whose interest it was to prolong the war longer than it was necessary, inevitable?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. Did you see the reason or reasons why the peace was not achieved earlier, or, rather, in whose interest was -- it was to prolong the war longer than it was inevitable or necessary? What powers and what domestic elements were for the prolonging of war?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I think the situation in the former Yugoslavia in different republics was very complex, and the reasons for the conflict or the prolongation of the conflict are numerous. There were domestic as well as international reasons. There were political, economic, social, historical, and many factors involved, and I don't think it is in my capacity to succinctly explain the causes of that most unfortunate war. I think opinions are divided, some emphasise international factors, others emphasise internal factors as more important for the conflict. And I simply point to these difference to say that it's beyond my competence to point my finger to one or a few factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you written and published a book under the title "In the Valley Between War and Peace," Excellency?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: It was published in Japan, in Japanese, five years ago, I believe, and then it was translated into English about two years ago under my supervision. And I would not call it a book. I will call it a booklet. It's a modest piece of exercise on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we see in the courtroom 1D29269.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that the cover page of your book, Excellency?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: It seems to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have page 32 in the book. In the e-court it may be little bit higher number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, may I recommend your -- to your attention on third -- page 33 the -- in the middle of second paragraph it's written Bosnia, and then the main issue was that neither the Bosnian government nor the United States government wanted a long-term cease-fire at that juncture based on the view that the hold of militarily superior Serb forces over a vast territory of Bosnia should not be permitted to become permanent. Does it --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So it's actually on page 32 of the book as opposed to the e-court, and it's the second full paragraph from the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it jog your memory on the different interests of foreign elements and domestic elements in prolonging the war or in avoiding long-term cease-fires?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Are you reading from page 32 of the booklet?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we zoom in a bit further. Yes, that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Aha. Fine. Yeah. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: What is -- what is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question was whether this jog your memory on the accord of these foreign and domestic elements that were not interested in long-term cease-fires.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes. That was my interpretation of events at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency. I would like to see number 33 just for one telephone conversation between you and President Carter. This is the end of first paragraph on this page.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this cease-fire, four-month cease-fire called Carter's cease-fire, and that after you informed him that it is maintained, he said that it was the best Christmas for him?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. I remember my telephone conversation with President Carter. I called him in Atlanta where he lived, and although I must say that much of the spade work was carried out by UNPROFOR headed by myself for preparing for the four-month efforts to conclude this what we called Cessation of Hostilities Agreement. I think President Carter's visit to Bosnia was very much welcomed by you, sir, and -- but Bosnian government did not particularly appreciate Carter's visit. And I had instructions from UN headquarters to brief him fully on my negotiations, which I did, and so I think President Carter made his contribution, particularly to your side, but I think I must say in all modesty that it was the UN which was basically behind this four-month agreement, but I felt that the visit by President Carter and his wife was a gracious act which facilitated acceptance of the agreement by your side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I tender those two pages and cover page of the book of Excellency Akashi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In case of the previous document we admitted as Exhibit D3488, I instructed the Registry to include page 2 so that we know a bit more about the detail, about the nature of the document. So in the case -- in this case we'll admit those two pages, and in addition we'll admit the first four pages to know what this document is about, to know the table -- to include table of contents.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Indeed, and frankly the Prosecution has no objection to the book in its entirety if it assists the parties in understanding the context of these remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us see how it evolves. So we'll admit first five pages and these two pages. Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3489, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I comment on this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. I would also much prefer that the whole booklet be available to the -- to this Chamber rather than any portion thereof, because unless the whole thing is read together, I think the contextual meaning may be distorted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Rest assured, Ambassador Akashi, the Chamber will have a hard copy in its entirety, but for the moment, for the purpose of the exhibit, we'll leave it as it is now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, how did you see the development of balance of the power or of the armed forces in former Yugoslavia, particularly concerning Bosnia and three sides in Bosnia? Was it the same all the time or was it shifted in one or another direction?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, the balance of power, more particularly in this case balance of military power, was constantly shifting. In the beginning of the conflict, the Bosnian Serb forces were predominant. At one stage they were in control of more than 70 per cent of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but towards the end of the conflict, after maybe 1994 and certainly in 1995, balance of power was gradually shifting for -- in favour of Bosnian government side, and also Croatian government was gaining in advantages towards the end of the conflict. That's why, I think, the Bosnian Serb side wanted more permanent, longer period of cease-fire and stabilisation of the situation, while Bosnian government was against the -- any kind of a long-term sort of freezing of the military situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have page 103 in the book of Ambassador Akashi. This is 1D29269, page 103.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, do you remember that there was an arms embargo for former Yugoslavia, but nevertheless, there was a change of balance and development in the status of armament of the sides?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask you to see the first paragraph of page 103 on the -- you can see it on the -- on the screen in front of you and particularly the end of this paragraph which says: "But as a result of active military assistance from the United States, Germany, and the Islamic states to Croatian and Bosnian forces, the overall power balance drastically shifted in favour of Croatia and Bosnia against Serbia in the four years between 1992 and 1995." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I tender this page to be added or have new number. I suppose to be added to the previous number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. For the moment we'll add this page to the previous exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, after you did assume your duties as a Special Representative of Secretary-General, have you received any assessment of your military commanders about the country that you have taken duty in? Have you got some briefings from your commanders?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question, please, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When -- after you assumed your duty, whether you got any assessment of -- from your commanders, commanders of United Nations that have been already in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes. It is a part, a very important part of my job to ensure that the civilian and the military components of the peacekeeping operation will be -- will have the same joint assessment of the situation in our duty station and the interchange of opinions and assessment was constant endeavour on our part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have in the e-court 65 ter 06875.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, do you remember this communication of yours toward the Under-Secretary Annan and comprising the assessment of General Briquemont?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Let me see. Please give me a second. This is dated 15 January.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I do not have my immediate recollection of this cable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May we have the next page, please. This is sent to you on 9th of January, and could you please -- could we please see the whole page and then ... Excellency, do you remember this number 1 where the political evolution it says if at the beginning of the war the Bosnians wanted to maintain one multi national state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, they now very clearly want to create a Muslim state?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: And if we see the end of this document. Last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's signed by General Briquemont, and number 3 -- point 3, conclusion, says that "... my assessment is that UNPROFOR's mandate is today very ambiguous." And how does it all fit in your experience and do you remember this briefing report at the beginning of your mandate?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes. Now I remember this assessment made by General Briquemont, and as well as my conversations with him at that time. It was towards the end of his own term, and he was rather bitter about the position in which UN peacekeepers were placed in the situation. He felt that the mandate given to the peacekeepers by the Security Council was extremely ambiguous and almost impossible to implement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have the previous page. And, please, the middle of page -- third paragraph, "Nevertheless": "Nevertheless, the demilitarisation of Srebrenica and Zepa took place, but we could not achieve a total demilitarisation at this stage, which causes difficulties with the Bosnian Serbs." And three paragraphs lower, for a few months the BH units from Srebrenica have been shelling the BSA position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that you found at the beginning of your mandate that those questions hadn't been resolved?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes. I remember these were the views expressed quite forthrightly by General Briquemont. Probably he was more frank at this time, at the end of his [Realtime transcript read in error "this"] mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3490, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Excellency, how many times we met approximately, and did anyone of your team make any notes during those meetings?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Indeed, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did those notes and your impressions been reflected in your reports and communications with the New York UN seat?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe not always 100 per cent, but I think these reports were quite close approximation of my own impressions, which were still fresh at that time, while my memory today is somewhat fading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have in e-court 65 ter 01250.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By the way, Mr. President, there's a slight error in the verbatim record. I said that, "Probably he," meaning Briquemont, was more frank at this time, at the end of his mission" not "at the end of this mission."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask you to see this document and do you remember was it the first meeting of ours, so 9th of January, 1994?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I believe it was our first meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we see the lower part of this page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "At the end of our meeting he," should be me, "strongly pointed out that if a peace agreement," next page, please, "be reached soon, the RS would have to declare the war." Have you been aware, Excellency, that the Muslim side declared the war against us and we did not declare the war on the whole Republika Srpska against them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I would suggest that Dr. Karadzic rephrase his question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Okay. I'll leave that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what is your question with respect to this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this meeting, Excellency, and what was your impression about fate and an attitude toward the talks, peace? What was your first impression of those meetings of ours?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I think our first meetings, including this first one, was very useful to me to get to know your concerns, as well as your assessment of the situation and difficulties in which your side was faced with, and I appreciated the discussions which took place, while obviously I was not in full agreement with everything which was said by your Excellency and as well as by your colleagues on the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I -- may we see the rest of the page, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I just note, Your Honours and Dr. Karadzic, Ambassador Akashi is trying to find himself in the relevant document in a hard copy binder, and to save time and assist the Ambassador I have unmarked copies of these documents. Perhaps with the usher's assistance I could pass them to Mr. Akashi so he could see the documents as a whole when dealing with Dr. Karadzic's questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be very helpful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber has no difficulty with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just to make a small correction, the only marking on the document is always the 65 ter number on the document, otherwise they are completely clean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And this is 65 ter 01250.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, do you remember that at this meeting you have achieved a lot and got my consent to the activities of the United Nations, particularly on humanitarian and convoy issues and deployment of the Dutch unit in Zepa and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, particularly with regard to the rotation of UNPROFOR troops in Srebrenica was a major obstacle in UNPROFOR fulfilling its mandate, and so I was glad that at these meetings we were able to achieve agreement of Dr. Karadzic and the Bosnian Serbs to accept the rotation to Srebrenica. It used to be performed by the Canadian unit, but after departure of the Canadian unit from Srebrenica we had difficulties. I think among other countries Sweden was discussed, but in the end it was very difficult to find the replacement to the Canadians, but it was good of Denmark to finally come out and agreed to take over from Canadians, thus filling the void in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you say "Denmark," Mr. Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe it is in the point 9 and 10 of this document, so could we have next page. And -- and in point 10, there is your first impression about the working relationship that had been established. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I tender this document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3491, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did these impressions of yours were reflected in your book?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have page 77 of the same book, that is 1D29269.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Not to mention your impression about my size in the first sentence. Does this say that it was more than 20 times that we have met? Do you see, Excellency, in front of you?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have next page. And you noticed the atmosphere of these meetings of ours. On page 79 you remember that I cited Robert Frost, and in -- last paragraph on this page you said that I was formidable adversary in negotiations and tough debater, but you point out the humourous and good atmosphere there. But would -- was it a fact that you achieved always something visiting Pale and me, that you never left Pale with empty hands?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I -- I beg to -- to make a reservation. I'm not sure whether we can make a general statement that always I was able to achieve what I had wanted through our meetings and discussions. I like to believe that I had your co-operation and understanding, but subsequent to our initial meetings, I think, Dr. Karadzic, you recall more difficult meetings we had subsequently. And in this booklet, I also mention that we shifted from more informal discussions in a rather good working environment to a larger conference room, and you shifted from speaking in English to me. You shifted to Serbian language and resorted to interpreters, which made our interchange more formal, more formalistic, and in my opinion somewhat more confrontational. I regretted it, but I think it was your insistence maybe vis-a-vis your colleagues on the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I tender these three pages to be added to the previous number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do that for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, do you remember meeting President Izetbegovic and me on 1st of February, 1994, in the occasion of preparations for the Geneva talks on the 10th of February? If it would jog your memory, I could call 65 ter 09088 in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we see the bottom of this page. Number -- paragraph number 4. Do you remember that you are -- was -- you were informed by President Izetbegovic that they -- that he expressed increasing distrust about Geneva talks on 10th of February?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have next page, please. The two next pages, number 3. Point 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, you wrote in this paragraph your -- elements from your meeting with Prime Minister Silajdzic, and you wrote down that -- that he was even less enthusiastic about talks, and he said that it may be -- it could -- it may be the last time they would go back to Geneva.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have lower part of this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what was my attitude toward the talks? And I have in mind paragraph 11. It's about rotation of troops in Srebrenica and my -- my objections about non -- demilitarisation of -- was it very often issue of our talks, Excellency?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes. Demilitarisation of safe areas, including Srebrenica, was one of our preoccupations, and we never stopped pointing out that the lack of demilitarisation of safe areas is an indispensable component of the safe area concept itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have the next page, last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in paragraph -- at the end of paragraph 12, you noted our own legitimate concerns about possible abuse of the airport, but what would I like to -- what I would like to recommend to your attention is point 14 concerning the convoys and particularly protection of the minorities in Banja Luka from the extremists. Do you remember this --

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- subject?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: -- I do. You remember, Dr. Karadzic, that we discussed the question of my visit to Banja Luka quite a number of times, and you always promised to do your best to facilitate my visit there, but I also remember that I was never allowed to visit Banja Luka. This was my constant frustrations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have an impression, Excellency, that I was concerned about your safety if you visited Banja Luka without me? Did we mention that I should be with you?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I don't remember that particular matter, but I think on different occasions we discussed different modalities of my visit, and you said you are trying your best to facilitate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3492, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, that was the beginning of February of 1994. Do you remember two major incidents that happened on 4th and 5th of February, 1994; 4th of February was in Dobrinja, and 5th of February, Markale marketplace?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you order and did you get an investigation of this incident, and what was the result of this investigation?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I recall that there was much speculation in the media about the perpetrators of the horrible tragedy in the open market in Sarajevo, and within UNPROFOR itself there were all kinds of speculations. Therefore, I decided to establish an expert committee consisting of, I believe, five ballistic experts: Two of its members were from countries rather friendly towards the Bosnia government, two others were friendly towards Bosnian Serb side, and with a neutral and impartial chairman from Canada. And so I felt that the composition of this body should be acceptable to both sides, and they did study all aspects of the mortar incident at the market, but there was only one mortar which was -- which came to the marketplace, and it hit some structure before it landed on the ground, which made it very difficult for experts to judge precisely where that mortar came from. Usually they can determine the angle from the angle and the distance where a mortar or any other weapon was shot at, but in the experts' views, the -- the shot could have come either from Bosnian Serb side or from Bosnian government side in that -- in that whole area of probably -- a probable attack. And so the conclusion, which I accepted fully, was that the attack could have come from either side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 01252.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is your communication to Annan and Stoltenberg on 6th of February.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: And may we have second page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think this is D713 as well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: It may well have been, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It is so noted already, Exhibit D13 -- D713.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, may I ask you to see number 7, and was that what you just said about the conclusion over the responsibility for this?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you meet me and General Galic on the next morning? Did you discuss with us, and what was or own response to these allegations?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I remember, Dr. Karadzic, you told me that in your opinion it was the Bosnian government side which did the shooting. You were emphatic that it was not your side, but I didn't expect any other opinion from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you -- did you -- did you notice that we had been enthusiastic about forthcoming talks in Geneva, and on the contrary, you notify that Izetbegovic and Silajdzic were not?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes. I think our cables recorded faithfully the different positions held by your side as well as the Bosnian government side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have page 44 of the same 1D29269, book of Excellency Akashi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What page, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Forty-four. It was just what you have said, that you confirm that I emphatically denied the responsibility. So maybe we don't have to, but ... In the middle of second paragraph. I can tender this page. Excellency Akashi has said it before seeing this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, did you ask any question about this?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. He asked a leading question and then he showed the page of the book, and perhaps he could be encouraged to re-order and rephrase his question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I can read my question from line 6, 26 page: "Did you meet me and General Galic on the next morning? Did you discuss with us, and what was our response to these allegations?" I think it was not leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But what's the point of tendering this page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Well, I lost one or two minutes, but it really corroborates what Excellency Akashi said. It was reflected in his book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see here "General Gvero," not "General Galic."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, Excellency, you are right, but I think there are documents that mention General Galic too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on. Shall we move on?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, do you remember the name of the chief of this investigating team from Canada?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could it have been General Michel Gauthier?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Excellencies, I see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, do you remember following those -- this incident in Markale II, whether we have a series of meetings that led to some agreement between the two of us?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this agreement that according to which I accepted the grouping of our heavy weaponry, free patrolling of the UNPROFOR, and particularly do you remember that I reserved the right to take our weapon in the case of massive attack by the Muslim forces, the attack that UNPROFOR couldn't prevent or stop?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Just a second. Excuse me, Ambassador. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry for the interruption. I think that's a very leading question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Okay. Then I would like to see D842 in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Excellency, what do you remember about those talks?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I think I remember the gist of those talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber, please, what was the substance of those talks.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, your side was agreeable to a cease-fire, but Bosnian government side said that a cease-fire is not enough. They wanted it to be accompanied by some measures of disarmament, more particularly the withdrawal of heavy weapons which your side possessed in and around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this communication of yours to Annan and Stoltenberg on 21st of February? Could you please see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have a hard copy?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I do. I could offer it up if that's of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we see page number 2 in the e-court, and just to identify what was the title of this letter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this letter of yours, Excellency?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Which letter are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This document, meeting with Dr. Karadzic and Krajisnik and Galic on 18th of February in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: That's another document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would the usher be able to assist Ambassador Akashi. I have given him a copy of the document with the page that we see now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But in the meantime, could you see -- do you see the document on the monitor? Mr. Karadzic is referring to this document. Probably that should be the second payment of the document Ms. Edgerton handed over to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have it now, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we see paragraph 4 on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Excellency, that I proposed the type of Sarajevo agreement to be suitable for the entire Bosnia as you state -- said in this paragraph 4?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could we have next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And for you also 3 -- page 3 of 6.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, do you remember in paragraph 6 that it was understood that we had a right to withdraw our weapons in the face of a massive attack? "It was hoped that such an eventuality would not occur as it would indicate a total breakdown of the peace." But do you remember that we had a right to acquire our own weaponry in the case that we attacked?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: No, but the UNPROFOR would be having a sort of intermediary presence between the two forces with its own troops, and each collection point will have such a presence, and for either side to attack any of these collection points, it will constitute a challenge to the United Nations itself. So we were endeavouring to make our presence so significant as to make it unnecessary for any side to challenge UN presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could we see point 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Excellency, that big concern of ours was the possibility that Muslim side attack the UNPROFOR on the Serb territory for the purpose of blaming the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I think that was one of your apprehensions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember the agreement that we have signed on 18th of February?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we see 65 ter 1D25260. I believe we have signatures too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is D717.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we see next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, do you see the number 1 in this protocol that regulates our right to self-defence in the case of the withdrawal of the interposition -- UNPROFOR from the interposition areas and in the case that UNPROFOR is not able either to prevent or stop attack, the Serbs reserves -- reserves the right to implement adequate measures of self-defence?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember, Excellency, that we met on 19th of February and that I proposed opening of routes to Sarajevo with the joint check-points of VRS H -- BH Army and UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Where is the reference, Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Not in this text, Excellency, but this is D716.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was there no question about D717?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think there was, and the answer was yes in line 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Ah, confirming that he saw the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I believe it was not that Excellency Akashi have seen it but that he participated in concluding this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we see for a moment D716. May we see then page 2, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, do you now remember, Excellency, number 3, what I proposed and what I expressed?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Mm-hmm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the other side accept this proposal of mixed check-points with the participation of UNPROFOR, BSA, and BH Army?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I don't believe they did. And in this connection, one of the major disagreements between the two sides, Bosnian Serb side and the Bosnian government side, was the number of weapons collection points. While Bosnian Serb side wanted as many collection points as possible, Bosnian government side wanted fewer, much fewer, number of such points, so that UNPROFOR better protect these points or centres with more troops, but Bosnian Serb side wanted a dispersal of these points so that they might have easier access to these sites. So we had to search for compromise between two sides and in the end I believe we settled on seven points.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency. May we have last page, paragraph 7. Do you remember, Excellency, your conclusion and observation of the tendencies of the Bosnian side to -- to feed the incident-hungry press in Sarajevo, and was it an obstacle for our doings on the bringing about peace?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I don't think I can answer such rather general questions. I'm not -- I was not very pleased with the press which had a tendency to capitalise on the differences between the two sides, and they tended to exaggerate the nature of incidents so that they can sort of sensationalise their nature. But we live in a world in which the press is always hungry for incidents and some unusual things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you write something about these moments in your book?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I remember having referred to the nature of mass media. This is one of the problems of democracies in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency. Have you learned, Excellency, that some of the generals, at least two of them, MacKenzie and -- and Briquemont, have noticed that the Bosnian side was abusing the public and sensitive spots and institutions and hospitals and schools, and UN facilities to fire against the Serb side from the vicinity of those spots in order to get retaliation and to blame the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yep, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Facts not in evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's an objection at this Tribunal, but Dr. Karadzic is putting a proposition to the witness. He can accept or reject. I don't see why it requires that the facts be in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees with Mr. Robinson. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you remember the question, Mr. Ambassador? Shall I ask Mr. Karadzic to repeat his question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting for translations, so that's why ... Excellencies, have you learned that some generals, at least two of them, General Briquemont and General MacKenzie, witnessed the government forces carrying out artillery attacks from the vicinity of very sensitive public buildings and UN facilities?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes. I think I heard observations from General Briquemont directly. As to General MacKenzie he had already left the duty station. Briquemont may have referred to what General MacKenzie had said, but I heard similar remarks, similar to General Briquemont from a few other military senior officers who are serving with UNPROFOR in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: And either to call in the courtroom e-court or to admit, I recommend page 110 of the Excellency Akashi's book which on this pages it is what -- exactly what Excellency Akashi confirmed now. Or can we see the number. Can we see the number 110 of this 1D29269.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you, Dr. Karadzic, referring to the first paragraph of page 110? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Exactly. What -- you have it on the -- on the screen.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes. I'm reading actually the paragraph from the booklet. That's why I feel that wars are horrible and we should do everything to avoid it and resolve it if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we see just the bottom of this page and also 111.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, this is the chapter of your understanding of the ethnic conflict, and did you hear that over more than 600 years there were grounds for the antagonisms of those ethnic groups as you said in the middle of this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes. I find it most unfortunate that some politicians do have extraordinary memory. They like to dwell on mistakes of all kinds from other parties, and instead of looking to the future, they tend to look at the past and let the past decide on their action for the future. I have coped with not only -- with this state of mind in the former Yugoslavia but elsewhere in the world. I think the more thoughtful people have to exert their influence, their wisdom so that politicians do not continue to indulge in -- in the past acts by other parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency. May we see page 111, the top. Do you remember, Excellencies, that you have concluded that the involvement and helps from outside worsened this situation in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that you have noticed that, for instance, Croatian and German governments by -- by premature recognition of Croatia, German government, then in Bosnia, worsened the situation, and particularly what you said the interval of the United States provided military assistance to Bosnia and Croatia and so on?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: These are my commentaries, and I agree with the observations of quite a number of people that these European governments should have heeded the very wise advice offered by the Badinter Commission of the European Union and should have made sure that their constitution should have provided for the vital interests not only of the majority group but minority groups. I think I say in this booklet that democracy consists of two pillars, majority decision and respect for minorities. I think we have to have those two pillars, and democracies cannot stand on one pillar alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I tender those two pages to be added or given another number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will add two e-court pages, i.e., e-court page 57, 58, which covers two subsection, i.e., fog of war and the way to ethnic conflicts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Was it 110 or 111?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It covers those pages.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, do you remember did we exchange letters when we were not able to meet, and do you remember that your letter of 27th -- 26th of -- of February?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I call, please, 1D02534.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Excellency, that I responded to your letter from 24th of February, and do you remember receiving this letter of mine?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I do not recall specifically this letter. We have exchange -- we did exchange a lot of letters at different times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you -- may I recommend to your attention third and fourth line in first paragraph: "We have stressed several times in our recent meetings with you that the Serbian side intends to fully implement the terms of ... agreement ..." And then first line of second paragraph that: "We, too, are anxious to ensure the return of normality within Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And, please, last paragraph. You are welcome to Pale, and what we said, that we highly appreciated your personality and your efforts. Don't you remember that?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, do I.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I tender this letter, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3493, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, do you remember an incident that occurred between Serb forces and the UNHCR convoy near Teslic which I investigated and confirmed that was -- actually happened?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have in the e-court 65 ter 01263.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your report to the United Nations about your letter to me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Can we have second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that your letter that concerns this incident?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm not objecting to the tendering of the document, but it's not a report of the ambassadors to the United Nations. It's, if we go back to the first page, a letter to the UNMOs in Pale asking that this protest be delivered to Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I apologise, yes, but also to the information of General Rose and UNPROFOR, Zagreb UNPROFOR, Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3494, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you. May way see now 65 ter 01265.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And this is my letter to you in response to your letter of 24th of March. May we have second page, please. Do you remember, Excellency, that I admitted that this incident appeared and assured you that that was not the manner that the VRS generally behaved?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I think your assertion is reflected in this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I tender this letter, this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3495, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I -- I believe, Excellency, that I have to skip the subject of Gorazde, and I regret for that, because it was quite a specific experience for both of us. Do you remember the crisis around Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I do remember, and, in fact, I -- I have not a very good memory of those incidents around Gorazde, and I remember particularly with deep regret that some of what you said to me was not reflected on the ground situation. And I remember our discussions in Geneva. We were staying in the same hotel, Hotel Intercontinental, and you told me a number of things your side was doing or had done, but upon checking, UNPROFOR on the ground, what you told me was not the real picture on the ground, and I found disconcerting these discrepancies between what you said, what you told me, and what was actually taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, could you always achieve everything that you wanted?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Could you repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As a civilian chief of the UN army there, could you achieve everything that you wanted?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I think at least I could count on UNPROFOR troops to observe the directives from their superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I see -- may we have 65 ter 11049 -- 48.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit D705, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Oh, right. Right. I see it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just to relax situation a little bit, Excellency, you see in paragraph 1 when the situation was very serious, Vice-President Koljevic was not between quotations. He was real vice-president, not so called vice-president.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we see paragraph 3 and 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Excellency, it said in line 2, paragraph 3, that although I gave you the assurances, there was a skirmish around Gorazde; and paragraph 4 that I stated that situation in Gorazde was a result of Muslim attack on BSA forces from the area and natural response -- Serb response was to attack? And do you remember me saying that it was common that Muslim strategy was they attack, we defend ourselves, and then they cry?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I agree with your assertion. I think it's a general statement which is not applicable in all concrete instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But do you remember that they caused by their own attacks to Gorazde, to the Serb territory, they caused this skirmish and that you have seen the same pattern of attacking from other safe areas to the Serb territory and that you have noticed it and notified the United Nations about that?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Now, I think each instance has to be examined on its own merit, and I think there are infringes on both sides. So I would not make a sweeping statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May we see paragraph 10. Do you remember, Excellency, that you urged me to allow ICRC to evacuate a great number of Muslims from Prijedor? And it had been notified in this paragraph 10. It was April 1994, two years after the beginning of the war. There were thousands of Muslims still in Prijedor, and not only Muslims but Muslim armed groups that massacres six policemen from the town. Do you remember that I was opposing -- maybe have next page. I opposed the idea of evacuation, and then I accepted to have several trucks a day, several.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that in the end we agreed on sort of a pragmatic, step-by-step solution to that crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you remember - this is paragraph 20 and 22 - that I accepted your proposal for the resolution of Gorazde crisis about exclusion zone and withdrawal of the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: You talk about your agreement but the most important negotiation to resolve Gorazde crisis took place, if I recollect, in Belgrade in the presidential residence of Mr. Milosevic, in which the Bosnian Serb side was represented by you, by General Mladic, and a number of others. UN side was represented by myself, by the force commander, and against a number of others. After some strenuous negotiation, I proposed that we have a small group consisting of President Milosevic, your Excellency, and General Mladic on your side, and the force commander and myself on the UN side, and in the -- in the midst of our negotiation, I came to receive information that NATO council reached -- had reached a very important decision on -- on the use of airpower if necessary to resolve Gorazde crisis, and you might remember rather strong remarks I made that you are faced with a historical decision which was very vital for the history and the welfare of the Serb people, and President Milosevic immediately understood the serious of the situation and it was due to his dominant leadership over the Bosnian Serb side that Bosnian Serb side decided to accept the proposal which UN side made. And it was after ten hours or even longer decision that at night we came to agreement, and in the next morning we were able to sign a written text of our agreement. Then I looked at my wristwatch, and I had only 20 minutes or so before the dead-line which I was given by UN headquarters to conclude our negotiations, but having had this agreement I felt I was able to stop the implementation or implication of the NATO air strike which could have been a real tragedy for the entire people. But I was blamed by some people, including some people in a very senior position in NATO for allowing Serb people to get away from this crisis. I did not because -- share that viewpoint of these people. But UN was placed in a difficult position for trying to resolve the crisis through diplomatic negotiations, but I'd like to note the fact that President Milosevic was very influential in these negotiations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency. Nevertheless, there was a NATO strike authorised by you which caused some standstill in our relations. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I do remember. And, Excellency, I must recall that repeatedly I told you -- I wrote to you about the difference between an air strike which is a full scale use of airpower, and close-air support, which is a more limited act of self-defence when UN personnel were faced with the mortal danger from weapons. And in those cases, invocation of close-air support was permitted when the smoking gun, so to speak, can be observed not only from the air but from the ground by the reconnaissance people on the UNPROFOR side. So it is unfortunate if you did not understand this distinction which we tried to make on every opportunity possible, in writing as well as verbally in our meetings as well as in our telephone -- numerous telephone conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency. When I said that we highly appreciated your attitudes, it doesn't include that you have been for the Serbs or softer to the Serbs. On the contrary. Assuming that we were stronger side, you were more tough towards us than two of the other sides.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Thank you for recognising my impartiality, and it is not always easy to maintain such a moral attitude, but I think it is professional pride for international civil servants like myself to adhere to the position of impartiality whenever occasion permits us to do. But for parties in a conflict, it is very easy to blame UN for doing something or for not doing something.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 01271.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, your answers are really precious for me and the, I suppose, other participants, but if we intend to finish this week, I would ask you whenever it is possible to give the shortest answers, the -- possible.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I will try my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this report of yours to Annan, Gharekhan and the others concerning the events of 15th and 16th April 1994?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we just go up so the Ambassador can see the signature on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably we can show the next page to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this chronology, Excellency?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Not all of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have this 1827 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yeah, "Serbs advise that they are concerned with our helicopters may be engaged overflying BH territory, and they will be --" the Serbs will be blamed.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have top -- bottom of this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember us being on the communication, radio communication, with the terrain? Your commander and my commander were over there, and two of us and Stoltenberg and Churkin were at Pale. And do you remember that there was a big conclusion about who was where? And it is the last paragraph here. Do you remember that it was confusion that military observers were unnotifying -- unnotified and unmarked on the first line and they all of a sudden appeared to be surrounded by the Serbs forces who did not have any idea that they are there?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that on the basis of our animated conversation you ordered General Mladic to stop firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection to the admission of entire document?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3496, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we show the last page of this document to the witness. Sir, do you confirm this page as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question of president was I believe to you, whether you authorised this page, and it looks like your recommendation what should be included in the Secretary-General's statement.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes. I recognise this paragraphs with couple of points we included in the statement to be made by the UN Secretary-General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have now 65 ter 01272.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your communication to Annan concerning the Gorazde crisis. May we see the middle of the page. That is concerning meeting with me and Krajisnik, Koljevic, and Gvero. And in paragraph 2 you notified -- noticed that the -- responded positively on withdrawal of heavy weapons, and there are points that were included, what we have agreed on. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow the question. Could you repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Well, maybe I was confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, may I draw your attention to the sixth line in paragraph 2 that you -- 6, 4, and 5 -- line 4, 5, and 6, that you are not -- that you written down that we responded positively about the withdrawal of heavy weapon, and you number several issues that we have agreed to.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes. I think this was what we were able to achieve after much discussion, and as I said here, this was the absolute minimum, not maximum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see second page. As you said, Excellency, when we have compromises, no maximums to any side. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I think the -- it depends on the situation, concrete situation we faced at different times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, do you -- do you remember that the Bosnian Muslim leadership was disappointed and they expected and wanted more robust involvement of NATO?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I tender this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect, and I could take it up in cross-examination if Your Honours wish, but I think that the Ambassador should have an opportunity to look at the document as a whole, and we haven't seen paragraph 3 -- or he hasn't seen paragraph 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think he remembers what the document contains, and if necessary, you may take up that issue. We'll receive it. In any event, the whole document will be an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3497, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, Mr. President, it's important for us to look at paragraphs in the context of the whole text always.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
