utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I read it. It continues on from the previous page, the last line on page 1. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did we meet, Excellency, on 22nd of April in Belgrade with Generals Mladic and Gvero and President Milosevic, discussing who was launching attacks and discussing the ability to monitor and accurately report who was attacking?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Could you repeat yourself, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember -- do you remember our meeting on 22nd of April, 1994, in Belgrade where I claim that the BH Army launching attacks from the safe areas and that I seeked and requested the UN to proceed immediately to Gorazde to be able to accurately report who was attacking?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I think in our meeting on the 22nd of April, 1994, we discussed many things. That meeting started at 12.00 noon and went on until 11.30 that night. So it was a marathon negotiation. We discussed many, many things centering, of course, around Gorazde crisis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I observe that Ambassador seems to be consulting some document when answering the question. So for record, could I ask you if you are relying on some handwritten notes or whatever? Could you clarify, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, yes. I was consulting a diary which I was writing major events of different days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. The Chamber sees no difficulty with it, but please let us know when you need to take a look at your diary, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your kindness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you. May we -- may we see in the courtroom 65 ter 18169.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this communication of yours to Annan on 23rd of April?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could we see the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, do you see those three bullets, normalisation of relations, solution to the crisis in Gorazde, and discussions on elements for the agreement on an overall cessation of hostilities?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And may we see -- may I draw your attention to paragraph 3 where I complained about criteria for safe areas which did not meet the requirements of the international conventions.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes. I think that you made a number of important points at our meeting on that day, and the question of safe areas was also one of the priority concerns of UNPROFOR. And in the -- in many of the reports to the Security Council by the Secretary-General, reference was made to these problems, most of which were equally applicable to all six safe areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you see, "As a result...," the sentence: "As a result, the BSA would not implement any cease-fire agreement in the enclave without the prior presence of the UNPROFOR to observe and report on the violations by either side"? Do you remember that we wished the presence of UNPROFOR in hot spots?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure whether I can give an unqualified yes to your question, but, yes, in several cases you are, of course, troubled by the alleged violations of safe areas by the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Can we see last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it -- was that agreement that you concluded with the Serb civilian and military authorities concerning this crisis?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes. It was after much difficulty that we were able to hammer out this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3498, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may make a short comment. I think after the Sarajevo crisis of February 1994, this Gorazde crisis was another example of resolving a serious crisis through our patient negotiations but under the threat of NATO air strike but without having actual air strike. Prior to that we were able to use diplomatic negotiations, however difficult they were, to achieve our final objective of peace. But to my profound regret it was not a lasting peace but a temporary peace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, when you mentioned the threats, was the other side also under the threats of the NATO attacks?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: It was our consistent position that if there are violations, infractions by either side, UN should take a decision for the use of airpower on an even, balanced, basis. The -- some of the Security Council resolutions have clauses talking about applying airpower equally to the parties, not a party, not one single party. But this position of UNPROFOR was not always shared by NATO or by some governments, and this -- this is a matter of disagreements within the UN or within the international community which may have weakened the final position taken by the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency. Do you remember that you had protested to Silajdzic about the presence of BH heavy weapons in the exclusion zone?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Which exclusion zone are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now we are -- about Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I think it was not just one time but a number of times we did lodge protests to the violations by the Bosnian government as well as by your side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we see, please, 65 ter 01276.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember your reports on meeting on 3rd of May, 1994,. Meetings with Prime Minister Silajdzic and me?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, with all respect, we can see, can we, from the paragraph 2 that it was for you much easier to get something for me -- from me to agree than from Silajdzic?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: You were understand me if I refrain from giving you a straight answer. It's not an easy job for -- to maintain a position of willingness to negotiate with all parties in conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 3 is concerning your concern over the discovery of BH heavy weapons and also of presence of seven BH Army weapons in contravention -- contravention to the Sarajevo agreement.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And may we -- may we -- yeah. You do remember that, yeah?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: And may we have page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the end of paragraph 11 do you remember that 500 Bosnian pilgrims departed to Mecca according to your agreement with me?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I do not have a specific recollection.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Okay. Can we have page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And at the end of paragraph 2 and -- it's concerning total exclusion zone, and you'll note that the UNPROFOR had under the terms of Security Council Resolution 913, requested the BH to put its heavy weapons under UN control.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did they, Excellency?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I do not recall in this instance what BiH did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3499, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: It's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. If it is convenient we'll take a break for 45 minutes and resume at 17 past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, your Excellency. I'll be ready in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, there are too many precious documents of your provenance and also all of your answers are very precious, but I wanted us to finish examination-in-chief today so that tomorrow you would be accomplishing your evidence, so I will try to be less confused in order to enable you to give very short answers. Do you remember our meeting of 5th of October, 1994, and after which you gave a statement and we have been talking a lot of topics? If it would jog your memory, I would like to see 65 ter 09670. This is your report from this meeting of 5th of October, and do you remember that we have been talking about peace plans and that I confirmed to you that we do not intend to divide city of Sarajevo but to form twin city?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could we have page 9 of 10. And at bottom of -- of page where I complain that United States does not want the end of the war yet. And I continued to say that there were fair solutions to be offered we would find for it in a -- in our parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was your insight, your experience with the -- with internal opposition that you mentioned in several documents, internal position to me that I had to convince people?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I think existence of divergence of opinions is to be found almost everywhere, but in the case of UNPROFOR, the difference of opinions was not based on the difference of their basic interest but honest difference with regard to the assessment of the situation and policies to be applied to cope with the situation. So I'm not sure whether this is the kind of situation in which you find yourself on the Bosnian Serb side. And within UNPROFOR there was an honest exchange of views, and we usually resolved it through our internal discussions, but with regard to the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina and more particularly with regard to how to cope with your side, the -- General Smith who succeeded General Rose was of the opinion that there should be more straight confrontation with your side, and so we tried to have continuous dialogue between our colleagues in Sarajevo and those of us in Zagreb, and that continued, and even the media started to speculate about these differences, but I find that they tended to exaggerate our differences internally. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that I mentioned to have twin city, to make two cities of Sarajevo and one to be Serbian to be -- to comprise the Serb suburbs?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Excellency, that we have been ready to give up territory for the peace that we did not claim to keep all territory that we controlled?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3500, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have 09671.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the crisis around -- around Igman, Mount Igman, when we withdrew in 1993 and have given this territory to the UNPROFOR and Muslims abused this area?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes. UNPROFOR was in frequent negotiation with -- with the Bosnian government side with regard to Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that they abused this area handed over to the United Nations, as a matter of fact, demilitarised and killed about 20 Serbs, mainly medical workers, and several females, mutilating them and so on? Do you remember this horrible event?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Can we have 12 out of 19 page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Dr. Karadzic. My notation may be mistaken, but I thought this might be P2439, this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The e-court says so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Then I apologise. We don't have to spend a lot of time on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you remember what was -- what is in this paragraph at the top about how those people had been executed? Lower half of the first paragraph. Excellency, it's not too important to study the whole document, just about this -- since this document is admitted, and it is of your provenance, do you remember how it was horrible and how it influenced Serbian side and aggravated my position with my army and with my people?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember the -- the Bihac crisis in November prior to President Carter's cease-fire? Do you remember that we exchanged some letters concerning Bihac?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have in the courtroom 65 ter 11608.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Second page is the original, but it's not legible, or it was rewritten on the first page. Do you remember my letter to you at that time?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have this letter admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So -- excuse me. So what you said is the original letter which is on the second page is illegible, so you quoted the content of that on the first page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I think somebody had rewritten. Can we see second page. I think it is the same content, and somebody had written it, retyped it, so to be legible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Any objection, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit D3501.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you may we have now 1D02477.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was from Pale to you to BH command.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: And please, could we have second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that I notified you that from -- from inside the safe area of Bihac they have been attacking us, meanwhile claiming that we are -- have been inside for 4 kilometres? And they have launched big offensive from Bihac taking almost 300 square kilometres of the Serb territory and when we made a counter-offensive then they have been threatening many threats by NATO, by ...

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: The Bihac situation was extremely complex and confusing, and the existence of Abdic and his troops made things even more confusing, and we were faced with constant complaints by the Bosnian government side about incursions from Bosnian Serbs. So we were trying to follow events closely, but our ability to observe closely was not of the maximum efficiency. But, of course, we had a commitment to stabilise the situation and not to aggravate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have the bottom of this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you notice that I regrettably informed you that if we are attacked, we have to treat forces that attacked us as our enemies?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I tender this letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3502, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could we have now 1D25264.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this draft of agreement, peace agreement, for the -- the new year, which was in the presence of President Carter?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could we have next page, please. There is a small handwriting, "We agree that we shall while the cessation of hostilities in effect negotiate," and so on. Can we have the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember now that was the first signature of this agreement by me, Mladic, and President Carter?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I don't remember this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you do remember, do you, the event, the conclusion of this agreement of which President Carter told you that it was the happiest Christmas for him?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: What he said to me on the 24th of December on the phone from me was that he was very happy to hear the news of agreement between UNPROFOR on the one hand and three parties in the Bosnian conflict that they will abide by the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement for four months starting from January 1st, and this was what UNPROFOR had been working for months, and I think President Carter gave you at least his -- his blessing to being a party to that agreement. This is not any kind of a peace agreement, but it's a four-month Cessation of Hostilities Agreement. But I worked very hard for that, and even it was only for four months, it was better than continuous fighting and high tensions between the parties. But you remember at the end of that period in April 1995 I tried my best to resuscitate that spirit of compromise and cessation of hostilities by replacing this agreement with another four-month agreement, and your side as well as Croatia -- Croatian Serb side -- Croatian side agreed to some kind of continuation, but Bosnian government was against continuation. So we could not have full agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3503, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I should have asked you, Ms. Edgerton, whether you have any objections.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that there was an additional agreement that was sent -- drafted and sent by President Carter himself? And if it would jog your memory, I would like to call 1D25265. Could we -- could we have -- it was -- it was sent to you from Mr. Andreev.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could we have next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And it was signed by me and by -- by President Carter and me, since in this phase it was a separate paper, signatures, on the both sides. Do you remember receiving this letter from Andreev?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I don't -- I do not remember this having been sent by my colleague Andreev.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have fifth page of sixth. This is in same wording, comprehensive peace agreement that President Carter signed with the Muslim side. Can we have last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you aware that it was signed that way? President Carter signed it with both sides separately?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I was not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we -- may I tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't think there's been sufficient comment in regard to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, apart from the comment, it does have all the indicia of reliability, and it was sent to Mr. Akashi, so I think there's a basis to admit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While Ambassador Akashi does not remember this letter he received, he would not challenge the authenticity of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no basis to agree with or to challenge the letter. I -- my office received only a copy of it. I was -- I was aware of the fact that the Bosnian government did not appreciate the visit by President Carter. They were irritated by his visit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3504, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember sending me letter in the occasion of these agreement expressing your appreciation for the efforts to conclude this agreement?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, you're referring to the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 06509.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine. Just understanding the agreement we've just seen is not the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement. The Cessation of Hostilities Agreement is P1648.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Sorry. The letter is 1D26684. May we have next page, please. We don't need the memorandum up there. Can we see the whole. And next page. And can we have next page and last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that you greeted, congratulated, and asked to commence these cessation of hostilities comments immediately?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and I remember expressing the hope that the step has been taken towards giving a new momentum to more permanent final peace and that this four-month agreement will be a useful way of consolidating the ground for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have this document admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3505, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: And finally all signatures on the same paper, could we have 06525. It is P1648 we learned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this final form of this agreement on complete cessation of hostilities? And if we may have last page, you will see who of us signed it. Do you remember, Excellency, that you have signed it, too, and your commander signed it too?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, commander for Bosnia and Herzegovina, not the force commander, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that it was altogether the most successful agreement on cessation of hostilities?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: It was a landmark of some kind. It was a great pity that it was not followed up with a more permanent step.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: This is already P, so ... May we have 1D03123.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how often this agreement had been violated and who led, who was relaying in these -- of these violations?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: In my memory, I think violations were committed by all sides, particularly by your side as well as by the Bosnian government side. Croats were sort of more or less on the sidelines on many occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I got what I asked for. I shouldn't asked a diplomat to say it, to say that. Do you see that General Mladic started to complain, to protest to the UNPROFOR about violations and -- violations of cease-fire agreement and relevant Security Council resolutions?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes. I think this matter was raised by General Mladic and by yourself also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have this document admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3506, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, do you remember what happened in February with -- with the Tuzla airport? Was there any crisis? Was there any -- were there any events that we complained about abuse of this airport?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: February what year?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: 1995. I do not specifically recall an incident in February 1995 with regard to Tuzla airport. The incidents at or around Tuzla were very frequent.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have in the courtroom, electronic courtroom, 1D03119.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a telegram of General de Lapresle to Annan concerning unidentified fixed-wing aircraft flights in Tuzla. And it says in paragraph 2 that ... [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And it says in first paragraph -- second paragraph that Norwegian air pilot on the ground observed transport type aircraft of C-130, and later, five minutes later, personnel was observed two jet aircrafts circling in the area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Can we have next page. Paragraph 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you see that NordBat APCs were dispatched there and have been -- while returning to the base, APCs were fired and subsequent surrounded by BH soldiers. Have you been informed about these observations of the events, unannounced and unauthorised events, on Tuzla airport?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in the comment it said it appears that two clandestine resupplies has taken place. The equipment delivered is assessed to be high value technology and so on. Do you remember, Excellency, that Muslim government opposed our own request to have our own observing officer at the airport Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: The question of monitoring the use of the Tuzla airport was the subject of our lengthy complex negotiations from the beginning of my mission. And I remember starting in January 1994 I negotiated with Prime Minister Silajdzic, with President Izetbegovic, as well as Vice-President Ganic, and I remember at one time I was embarrassed by the fact that what was accepted by Prime Minister Silajdzic was not endorsed but was contradicted by Vice-President Ganic. So I think Bosnian government was no exception to internal difference of views. But I think on your side also, Dr. Karadzic, the Russians proposed something different from your position would cut away that Tuzla airport was to be monitored. And while Russians supported your position in general, in this particular instance we felt that it was probably a lack of closer co-operation between Pale and Moscow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3507, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, could you tell us what was the assumption and knowledge of the United Nations? Who delivered this equipment and armament and to what side in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I think there was much speculation as to these unreported, unverified flights to Tuzla, but it remains in the realm of speculation. There was no way for us to ascertain where they came from and what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have now 1D03122. This is from 25th of February, protest from General Mladic, and may we have next page. And there's sort of draft of the response of General Smith, but can we have next page. Lower part of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Had you been informed about those objections and protests by General Mladic to General de Lapresle concerning Tuzla, the abuse of Tuzla airport?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I was generally aware of these complaints, but I did not have specific recollection of this instance of 23 February 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3508, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Excellency, whether our own meetings in March and the rest of the 1995 were frequent?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Were frequent did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean 1995, March 1995, were they frequent?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I think our meetings were much more frequent in 1994 rather than 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I call 65 ter 09749.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this report of yours concerning your meeting with Bosnian government officials, and do you remember that it -- this meeting of yours have treated a killing of two girls, 9 and 11, by sniper fire into Grbavica, Serb part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that it caused us crisis about routes and about communications in and around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I do not recall that, but this memorandum refers to an incident of my aircraft being machine-gunned as it was taxiing and landing at the Sarajevo airport, and General -- General Smith was convinced and was sure that it was the Bosnian Serb side who shot at our aircraft, and he lodge a strong protest to that, but I chose not to raise the matter with you, Excellency, because I was negotiating on political matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And this last sentence of -- two last sentence of the first paragraph, it says: "The purpose of the meetings was to encourage the Bosnian government to recommit themselves to the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement ..."

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How come -- does it mean they reneged from this agreement?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I think the fact of the matter was that the Bosnian government was not enthusiastic in the continuation of that Cessation of Hostilities Agreement beyond -- beyond that date of termination of that agreement at the end of April 1995. As you know well, the military balance of power was shifting in favour of the Bosnian government, so there was a lack of -- lack of enthusiasm for continuing that status quo ante.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I tender this document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3509, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 01325.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Of the same day reporting of your meeting with the Bosnian Serb officials --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P2479, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... and I apologise. Do you see that we have complained bitterly about alleged noncompliance of the Bosnian government about all aspects -- violating all aspects of the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we scroll down a bit on document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you said that Serbs have resistance to participate in any further meetings of the Central Joint Commission, and as it became evident that the difficulties with the implementation of the COHA are now of an essential political nature.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes. I think what it said was very clear. It was not a technical military question, but it's a question of political decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have 1D03440.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Excellency, that you succeeded again with me on the issue of exchange of prisoners of war? And here we have your letter to me in that -- in that sectors.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember writing this --

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- letter to me?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what was the attitude of the Muslim side concerning exchange of prisoners, and do you remember whether we succeeded to exchange people from Silos in Tarcin or to exchange all for all as we proposed many times?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I think the question of the exchange of prisoners of war and asking for support and assistance from ICRC was not a one-sided issue. I think ICRC had a very difficult job of interceding between the two contending sides. So I would not say that the matter of prisoner exchange was not a one-sided issue with a victor and a defeated. It varied from case to case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I tender this letter, this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3510, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, do you remember that we met on 20th of April, 1995, on the occasion of my complaints about Bosnian Muslims' non-compliance with the agreement and that I asked your Excellency and UNPROFOR to make them comply otherwise we would have to start to retaliate: Sniping and other assaults, and which would mean renewal of the war in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: One of the items in our bilateral negotiations was not tense -- I think there was a positive spirit there, but I thought that your overall position was quite non-compromising, and I remember having been troubled by your posture of defiance of the international community, and we were also of the impression that there was some kind of tension between your military and the civilian side. We noted that General Mladic was absent at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 01332.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your telegram concerning this -- this meeting, telegram to Annan, Stoltenberg, and others, and do you remember that we -- I complained a lot of violations and -- and developments that were very unsatisfactory for the Serb side? Let me see the whole first page and the next page. And do you see that we informed you that we are pressed by population and parliament to end non-beneficial relationship with UNPROFOR: "... UNPROFOR failed to pressurise the Bosnian side to respect agreements; sniping in Sarajevo could lead to renewal of war and was a form of ethnic cleansing of Serbs; Bosnian Serbs would force -- be forced to retaliate appropriately to Bosnian actions in Sarajevo, and this would mean a total war."

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, this is an annunciation of your own position, yeah. I hope we faithfully summarised your position and your arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And I draw your attention to the first line on the top of the page about our complaints that the airport was abused, being used as a taxi and ferry service for our enemies and the whole page is about my complaints, and number 6, Karadzic, "In response to Karadzic's skepticism of the role of UNPROFOR," you said -- what did you say about the task that UNPROFOR did? And may we have next page. Paragraph 7. I did not lack faith in your good intentions, but we held that we are not treated well and that sanctions committees not just towards us and so on. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3511, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: One moment, please. I ask you for indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm encouraging Dr. Karadzic to skip through so that we could finish with Mr. Akashi. So we'll just take one minute and try to shorten this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I do hope that the genuine UN documents, Excellencies, would be admitable through the bar table, so I would skip several subjects and documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excellency, have you been of -- did you have an opinion about possible advantages that Bosnian government have taken from six safe areas, including Srebrenica, in terms of resting troops, re-equip, retrain?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, and I already referred to some reports the UN Secretary-General submitted to the Security Council discussing the state of affairs with regard to six safe areas and for several defects or short-comings of the concept of the safe areas as well as the implementation. The Secretary-General had serious reservations about the soundness of the concept of safe areas, and among other matters, he raised the question of shortage of the necessary number of UN troops. He had originally asked from over 30.000 troops, of which only about 7.000 were approved by the UN General Assembly. And secondary, as Dr. Karadzic referred to, the one side in the conflict used the safe areas for rest, recuperation, and other purposes emanating from these safe areas. And thirdly, the disarmament provisions were not implemented, at different times and to different degrees. And lastly, there was no demarcation of these safe areas in most instances, and so Secretary-General was of the opinion that there was a basic defect to the concept as well as to the actual practice, but UN Security Council in its wisdom did not heed very much to these opinions of the Secretary-General. You might say that "faute de mieux" the international community as a whole felt that therefore the safety and security of innocent civilians in those safe areas it had to go along with it. But, you know, we were at the service of the international community and more specifically under the overall command of the UN Security Council. So the Secretary-General, despite his strong views about safe areas, he accepted the reality, political reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have in the e-court 1D07340, and then 6 and 7 page, first 6 and then 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is part of your testimony in the -- on the board of the French parliament, and you exactly said what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May we have the bottom of page. And may we have next page, please. Is that 6 and 7? Yes. First paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "... the Bosnian government took advantage of the six designated safe areas." So you were aware of that and you testified in the French parliament about that, and just exactly what you said the Secretary-General wanted to have it different.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Thank you. And may I receive a copy of my own statement at the French parliament committee. I don't have a copy myself, but I don't think I need to change anything contained in that statement of mine. France and the United Kingdom, among other countries, were very loyal and very faithful to the mission of UNPROFOR in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I tender those two pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's chapter 3 in the translated version. So no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this different from what we saw earlier in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That was chapter 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But in different 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Ms. Edgerton repeat it, because her microphone was off.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I said that was chapter 2. I'm sorry, I'm not familiar -- I didn't appreciate the difference in the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think it's the same, Mr. President. 7340.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the exhibit number we --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D3488, Your Honours, and page 6 was already admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But what I noted down was what we saw was 1D10513, the title of which was "Mr. Akashi answers to French parliament," and this is a bit different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that 1D10513 and 1D7340 are the same documents. Yes, we'll add these pages to Exhibit -- Defence exhibit. What was the number again? D3488. And the -- is the Defence going to deal with Mr. Ambassador's request to see the whole document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We can print out the entire document for him and give it to him. With your permission we can give it to him before he leaves today if we like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any difficulty with that, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. I have a copy here immediately if it assists.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If possible in English as well as in the original French version.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We have both.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was given in impeccable French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no doubt about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, Dr. Karadzic is about to get into the last area of his examination involving the events in Srebrenica, and I expect that this will take maybe about another 30 minutes, and I was wondering whether or not we should excuse General Galic for tomorrow given the fact that we've used up the whole day today with our direct examinational.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How long do you expect your cross-examination to last, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Up to this point, Your Honours, I was thinking an hour and a half or two hours, without having necessarily crafted questions. I think two hours is probably reasonable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Together with remainder of Mr. Karadzic's in chief examination, that will take up about two sessions. And Mr. Karadzic no doubt will need some time for his re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure he will. And I know it may give us a little bit of extra time, but since it is right before the break and given that Mr. Piletta-Zanin is able to return to Geneva today if we won't make him wait around, perhaps on balance it might be good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber finds the suggestion to be fair enough. I thank you for that. So we'll excuse General Galic for tomorrow. Given the time, shall we adjourn for today and continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador Akashi. We'll adjourn for today and continue tomorrow. Probably you will be well aware of this, but could I advise you not to discuss about your testimony with anybody else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
